# Abstract

Between the Lapita founding landfalls on Tongatapu and Upolu early in the first millennium BC and the closing decades of indigenous autonomy in 1800, Polynesian seafarers peopled an oceanic expanse stretching from the International Date Line to Rapa Nui. Covering nine archipelago sub-regions across 63.030,3 km² of buffered coastal and lagoon mask footprint (excluding Hawai'i and American Samoa, which belong to separate territorial domains), this study tracks population growth from an archaeological founding baseline of 4,5k in West Polynesia at 1000BC (35,7k in the continuous regional benchmark series when pre-colonisation initialisation floors are carried backward) to 34k across West Polynesia by AD 1 (65,2k harmonised), 126,5k by AD 1000, 193,2k by AD 1400, an eve-of-contact high of roughly 233k across all nine archipelagos in 1770 to 1780 and a closing total of 213,4k (213.400) in 1800 [@patrick2010peopling; @burley2012high; @wilmshurst2011high]. Demographic weight shifted decisively over three millennia. For nearly two thousand years after Lapita landfall, virtually all Polynesians inhabited Tonga, Samoa, Wallis and Futuna, where irrigated taro valleys, dryland yam gardens and reef fisheries nourished the rise of the Tu'i Tonga maritime chiefdom centred at Mu'a and monumental mound complexes such as Pulemelei on Savai'i [@burley2010nukuleka; @gallagher2022investigatin]. Rapid eastward voyaging across Central and Marginal East Polynesia between AD 900 and AD 1250 populated the Society, Marquesas, Cook, Austral, Tuamotu, Gambier and Rapa Nui archipelagos [@wilmshurst2011high; @ioannidis2021paths]. By 1770 to 1790, high volcanic archipelagos reached their pre-colonial demographic crest, led by the Society Islands (68k before falling to 42k in 1800 under early contact epidemics), Independent Samoa and Wallis-Futuna (46k), the Marquesas Islands (45k in 1790, easing to 38k in 1800), Tonga (36k) and the Cook Islands and Niue (21k), whereas low coral atolls in Tuamotu-Gambier (11k) and Tuvalu-Tokelau (5,2k) remained constrained by freshwater lenses and cyclone risk [@allen2025reciprocity; @kahn2013residential; @dinapoli2021approximate]. Across 67 catalogued settlements and 184 dated observations spanning ten modern states and territories, peak settlement sizes exhibit a flat chiefdom rank-size profile ($\alpha = 0,31$, $R^2 = 0,95$ across the top 33 centres) led by Mu'a (4,1k), Pare-Arue (4k) and Taipivai (3,9k).

# Background

## Lapita Foundations and the West Polynesian Homeland

Human settlement in Polynesia began with a sharp maritime leap out of eastern Fiji across the Andesite Line into the Tonga and Samoa archipelagos early in the first millennium BC [@kirch2017road; @patrick2010peopling; @cochrane2010evidence]. Unlike Island Melanesia, where Papuan-speaking populations had lived since the Pleistocene, every island east of Fiji was virgin oceanic terrain devoid of terrestrial mammals apart from bats. Colonising canoes carried a portable agro-ecological package combining taro (*Colocasia esculenta*), yams (*Dioscorea* spp.), breadfruit (*Artocarpus altilis*), banana, coconut, pig, dog, junglefowl and the commensal Pacific rat (*Rattus exulans*) [@matisoo_smith1996hea; @kirch2001hawaiki; @patrick2010peopling]. High-precision uranium-thorium dating of coral abrader artefacts from the Nukuleka founder settlement on the Fanga 'Uta lagoon of Tongatapu pins initial Lapita arrival to c. 888BC (2838 BP), establishing Tonga as the earliest securely dated Polynesian landfall [@burley2001origin; @burley2012high; @burley2010nukuleka].

From Nukuleka, pioneer communities fanned out within a few generations across Ha'apai (Pangai on Lifuka), Vava'u, Niuatoputapu (Hihifo), Uvea (Talietumu), Futuna (Sigave) and the submerged Lapita ferry-berth settlement at Mulifanua on western Upolu [@burley2010nukuleka; @gallagher2022investigatin]. Ceramic petrography and obsidian sourcing confirm active inter-archipelago voyaging across the Fiji-Tonga-Samoa triangle during this formative phase, moving volcanic glass from Tafahi in northern Tonga alongside finely tempered Lapita and Polynesian Plainware vessels [@reepmeyer2012obsidian; @gallagher2022investigatin]. Yet within four centuries of colonisation, potters across Tonga abruptly abandoned dentate-stamped decoration and subsequently ceased ceramic manufacture altogether, switching to earth-oven cooking (*umu*) and perishable wooden or gourd containers [@burley2018early].

During the ensuing millennium of relative isolation inside West Polynesia—often termed the Long Pause—settlers evolved Ancestral Polynesian Society, consolidating the Proto-Polynesian language, hereditary chieftainship (*ariki*), outrigger and double-hulled canoe architecture and specialised wetland and dryland horticulture [@kirch1992history; @kirch2001hawaiki; @patrick2010peopling; @matisoo_smith2026minding]. Comparative faunal assemblages from Samoan coastal sites show an initial phase of heavy reef-fish, turtle and seabird exploitation giving way to sustainable inshore fisheries and intensified root-crop cultivation as populations expanded inland from coastal beach flats into fertile volcanic valleys such as Falefa and Vailele on Upolu [@weisler2016colonisation; @gallagher2022investigatin]. By AD 1, Tonga held an estimated 16k inhabitants and Independent Samoa with Wallis-Futuna held 18k, establishing a stable West Polynesian core of 34k people well before the permanent peopling of the eastern archipelagos.

## Chiefdom Consolidation in Tonga and Samoa

Between AD 950 and AD 1500, demographic growth in West Polynesia supported unprecedented monumental architecture and long-distance maritime integration. On Tongatapu, the sacred dynasty of the Tu'i Tonga relocated its royal seat to Mu'a (Lapaha) along the sheltered shore of Fanga 'Uta lagoon around AD 1200 to 1300 [@clark2014stone; @burley2018early; @reepmeyer2012obsidian]. Over the next five centuries, corvée labour drawn from across Tongatapu, Ha'apai, Vava'u and outlying dependencies erected stepped royal burial tombs (*langi*) faced with quarried coral-limestone slabs, reclaimed tidal flats for canoe harbours and turned Mu'a into Polynesia's largest pre-colonial town, reaching 4,1k inhabitants by James Cook's visit in 1777. Through tributary voyages, marriage alliances and military garrisons—exemplified by the fortified stone compound of Talietumu on Uvea—the Tu'i Tonga polity projected influence over Samoa, Rotuma, Niue, Uvea, Futuna and eastern Fiji, moving basalt adzes, red feathers, mats and obsidian across thousands of kilometres of open ocean [@clark2014stone; @reepmeyer2012obsidian; @gallagher2022investigatin].

Samoa followed a parallel yet politically less centralised trajectory. Rather than coalescing under a single island-wide monarch, Upolu and Savai'i divided into fiercely competitive district paramountcies (*Atua*, *A'ana*, *Tuamasaga* and the Savai'i districts) anchored by dense inland plantation zones and coastal villages such as Leulumoega, Falefa, Vailele, Luatuanu'u and Safotu [@gallagher2022investigatin; @weisler2016colonisation]. On southern Savai'i, communities constructed the massive stepped basalt platform of Pulemelei in the Letolo district between AD 1100 and AD 1600, surrounded by hundreds of residential star mounds (*tia seu lupe*), paved walkways and house platforms capable of sustaining roughly 1,7k people at its 1500 peak [@wallin2007radiocarbon]. By 1800, Tonga had grown to 36k inhabitants and Independent Samoa together with Wallis-Futuna had reached 46k, forming the demographic anchor of western Polynesia.

## The East Polynesian Voyaging Pulse

After nearly two millennia confined to the western core, Polynesian navigators launched one of the fastest oceanic migrations in human history. High-precision radiocarbon re-evaluation of short-lived botanical samples has overturned earlier long-chronology models that placed Marquesan or Society Islands colonisation in the first centuries AD [@wilmshurst2011high; @petchey2020vital; @sear2020human]. Instead, strict chronometric hygiene indicates that canoes departed West Polynesia—primarily from the Samoan sphere—for the Cook and Society Islands between AD 900 and AD 1120, followed within two centuries by explosive outward radiation to the Marquesas, Austral Islands, Tuamotus, Mangareva, Pitcairn, Henderson, Rapa Nui, Hawai'i and Aotearoa New Zealand between AD 1150 and AD 1290 [@wilmshurst2011high; @sear2020human; @ioannidis2021paths].

Independent genomic and commensal lines of evidence corroborate this late, rapid branching topology. Genome-wide ancestry networks from modern and ancient islanders trace an eastward stepping-stone radiation out of Samoa through Rarotonga and the Society Islands, splitting northeast into the Marquesas and southeast through the Australs and Gambier Islands toward Rapa Nui [@ioannidis2021paths; @ioannidis2020native; @hudjashov2018investigatin]. Mitochondrial lineages of the Pacific rat (*Rattus exulans*) mirror the same central East Polynesian hub, confirming intentional return voyaging rather than accidental one-way drift [@matisoo_smith1996hea; @matisoo_smith2026minding]. Experimental sailing trials with reconstructed East Polynesian crab-claw and spritsail rigs further demonstrate that shifts in regional windward sailing technology and multi-decadal El Niño wind reversals periodically opened eastward voyaging corridors against the prevailing southeast trades [@anderson2011east; @rolett2002voyaging].

## High-Island Chiefdoms, Atoll Ecologies and the Eastern Margins

Once established across Central and Marginal East Polynesia, demographic outcomes diverged sharply according to island geomorphology. High volcanic islands with amphitheatre valleys, perennial streams and deep alluvial soils—above all Tahiti, Mo'orea, Ra'iātea, Huahine and Bora Bora in the Society archipelago, together with Nuku Hiva, Hiva Oa and Ua Pou in the Marquesas—supported dense agro-forestry combining irrigated pondfield taro, terraced slopes and extensive breadfruit groves [@kahn2013residential; @allen2022lost]. In the Society Islands, competing *ari'i* lineages organised society into stratified house estates (*fare*) centred on monumental stone temples (*marae*) such as Taputapuātea at Opoa on Ra'iātea, which served as a pan-Polynesian ritual hub linking Windward and Leeward elites, Cook Island voyagers and Austral navigators [@kahn2013residential; @weisler1998hard; @allen2025reciprocity; @mcgloin2026microwear]. By 1770, Tahiti and its neighbours held roughly 68k inhabitants, anchored by populous coastal chiefdoms at Pare-Arue (3,95k), Papara (3,45k), Opunohu on Mo'orea (3,24k) and Tautira on Tahiti Iti (2,89k).

In the rugged, reefless Marquesas, steep canyon topography split each island into fiercely autonomous valleys—such as Taipivai on Nuku Hiva (3,85k), Atuona on Hiva Oa (3,12k) and Hakahau on Ua Pou (2,64k)—sustained by massive subterranean breadfruit fermentation pits (*ma*) designed to buffer periodic multi-year droughts [@allen2022lost; @molle2011perspectives]. Early coastal dune settlements such as Hane and Hatuana on Ua Huka and Hanamiai on Tahuata document rapid transformation of pristine native palm forests and seabird colonies from the twelfth century onward, while basalt quarries on arid Eiao Island supplied high-grade adze stone across the entire archipelago and as far afield as the Society and Tuamotu islands [@rolett2002voyaging; @weisler1998hard; @molle2011perspectives; @lambrides2018taxonomic; @allen2025reciprocity].

Along the southern volcanic arc of the Cook and Austral islands—Rarotonga, Mangaia, Aitutaki, Rurutu, Tubuai, Ra'ivavae and Rapa Iti—growing populations cleared interior hillsides, excavated irrigated swamp taro flats and, on high Rapa Iti around Ahurei, carved ring-ditched hilltop forts (*pare*) during late pre-colonial resource rivalry [@kennett2006prehistoric; @kahn2026morphologica; @allen2025reciprocity]. On Rurutu, residential archaeology traces the evolution of rectangular and oval-ended stone house foundations (*paepae*) reflecting tight household spatial organisation around valley gardens [@kahn2026morphologica]. By contrast, low coral atolls across the Tuamotus, Tuvalu and Tokelau lacked surface streams and volcanic soils. Communities depended on excavated brackish-water taro pits (*babai* or *pulaka*), coconut groves, pandanus and lagoon fishing, holding individual atolls such as Anaa (Tukuhora), Rangiroa (Tiputa), Nanumea (Lolua) and Fakaofo to a few hundred or at most two thousand people [@petchey2010interpreting; @allen2025reciprocity].

At the southeastern vertex of the Polynesian Triangle, Rapa Nui and the tiny Pitcairn-Henderson group represented the limits of Polynesian agrarian adaptation. Settled around AD 1200, Rapa Nui's volcanic plateau lacked coral reefs and perennial rivers, yet islanders transformed cleared palm landscapes into lithic mulch gardens cultivating sweet potato (*Ipomoea batatas*), yams and taro while erecting nearly a thousand monumental *moai* statues on coastal *ahu* platforms at Anakena, Tongariki, Vaihu and Vinapu [@hunt2006late; @mulrooney2013island; @dinapoli2021approximate; @lipo2025megalithic; @mathiesen2020disputa]. Pre-Columbian dispersal of the South American sweet potato (*kumara*) into East Polynesia—and genomic evidence for early Native American contact alongside continuing debate over osteological markers along the Chilean littoral—testify to the extraordinary navigational reach of late East Polynesian seafarers [@roullier2013historical; @ioannidis2020native; @barber2021archaeologic; @buhring2020archaeology; @matisoo_smith2009human]. Meanwhile, Pitcairn and neighbouring Henderson sustained small trading outposts linked to Mangareva until regional exchange networks contracted around AD 1450, leaving Pitcairn uninhabited until *Bounty* mutineers and their Tahitian companions founded Adamstown with 27 settlers in 1790 [@weisler1998hard; @allen2025reciprocity; @flexner2026islands].

# Methodology

## Archipelago Partition and Domain Boundaries

To preserve ecological coherence across an oceanic realm of scattered volcanic high islands, raised limestone *makatea* islands and low coral atolls, AUSTRAL partitions Pre-Colonial Polynesia into nine archipelago sub-regions spanning 63.030,3 km² of buffered coastal and lagoon areal mask footprint from 1000BC to 1800. Two major Polynesian jurisdictions are deliberately excluded from this chapter's territorial mask: the Hawaiian Islands and American Samoa, both of which are modelled within the United States territorial framework of the northern Pacific, and Aotearoa New Zealand, which forms a dedicated companion chapter owing to its continental-scale landmass and temperate ecological regime.

The nine sub-regions group geographically contiguous archipelagos sharing common colonisation histories and subsistence regimes: Tonga Archipelago (5.173,1 km² mask area, encompassing Tongatapu, 'Eua, Ha'apai, Vava'u and the Niuas); Independent Samoa and Wallis-Futuna (6.338 km², covering Upolu, Savai'i, Uvea and Futuna); Society Islands, Windward and Leeward (6.400,3 km², covering Tahiti, Mo'orea, Huahine, Ra'iātea, Taha'a, Bora Bora and Maupiti); Marquesas Islands (3.475,2 km², covering Nuku Hiva, Ua Huka, Ua Pou, Hiva Oa, Tahuata and Fatu Hiva); Tuamotu and Gambier Islands (28.160,4 km², combining the extensive Tuamotu coral atoll chain with volcanic Mangareva); Austral Islands (4.987,2 km², spanning Rimatara, Rurutu, Tubuai, Ra'ivavae and Rapa Iti); Cook Islands and Niue (5.100 km², uniting the Southern and Northern Cooks with raised-atoll Niue); Tuvalu and Tokelau (2.550,2 km², combining the central Polynesian atolls); and Rapa Nui and Pitcairn (845,9 km²).

Because many Polynesian islands and coral atolls measure only a few square kilometres across—far narrower than a single raster cell on a global demographic grid—each sub-region's areal mask incorporates a standardised coastal and lagoon buffer so every inhabited archipelago remains spatially resolvable. Consequently, the 63.030,3 km² mask footprint exceeds Polynesia's strict subaerial terrestrial land area (roughly 6,5k to 7,2k km² across these ten jurisdictions) by almost an order of magnitude. All mask-footprint density values reported in tables and charts (3,39 inhabitants per km² overall in 1800, rising to 10,94 in the Marquesas) must therefore be read as archipelago-envelope densities, while terrestrial agricultural densities inside individual valleys and atolls ranged five to fifteen times higher [@kahn2013residential; @dinapoli2021approximate].

## Longitudinal Demographic Calibration and Carrying-Capacity Modelling

Pre-colonial Polynesian societies produced no written censuses prior to late eighteenth-century European voyages and early nineteenth-century missionary enumerations. Regional population curves $P_r(t)$ across the eight benchmark horizons ($t \in \{-1000, 0, 500, 800, 1000, 1200, 1400, 1800\}$) are reconstructed by triangulating three independent bodies of evidence: calibrated radiocarbon and uranium-thorium settlement chronologies [@burley2012high; @wilmshurst2011high; @petchey2010interpreting], archaeological household and agricultural carrying-capacity surveys [@kahn2013residential; @kahn2026morphologica; @dinapoli2021approximate] and critical demographic retrojection from the earliest contact-era counts and nineteenth-century colonial censuses [@flexner2026islands; @allen2022lost].

For each archipelago $r$, intrinsic growth between founding colonisation $t_0$ and pre-contact carrying capacity $K_r$ follows a damped logistic trajectory modulated by island ecological ceilings and documented late pre-colonial or early contact shocks:

$$P_r(t) = \frac{K_r}{1 + \left(\frac{K_r - P_r(t_0)}{P_r(t_0)}\right) e^{-\rho_r (t - t_0)}} \cdot \psi_r(t)$$

where $P_r(t_0)$ denotes the initial colonising cohort (typically 100 to 500 settlers across founder settlements), $\rho_r$ represents the net intrinsic rate of increase (0,2% to 0,5% per annum during early virgin-island expansion, tapering below 0,05% as valleys approached agrarian saturation) and $\psi_r(t) \le 1$ captures exogenous demographic contractions—most notably early European epidemic introductions in the Society Islands between 1769 and 1800 (reducing population from 68k to 42k) and in the Marquesas during the 1790s (45k to 38k), together with late pre-contact climatic and ecological adjustment on Rapa Nui (9,5k in 1550 to 3,2k in 1800) [@dinapoli2021approximate; @allen2022lost]. Compound annual growth rates between adjacent benchmark dates $t_1$ and $t_2$ are computed identically across all sub-regions:

$$g_r(t_1, t_2) = \left(\frac{P_r(t_2)}{P_r(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{t_2 - t_1}} - 1$$

An important accounting distinction separates the raw archaeological anchor series from the continuous interpolated benchmark series. In the raw archaeological anchors, all seven East Polynesian and central atoll sub-regions stand at strictly zero inhabitants at 1000BC, leaving only Tonga (2,5k) and Samoa with Wallis-Futuna (2k) inhabited (4,5k total). To maintain continuous log-linear interpolation across the chapter's eight benchmark columns without division-by-zero singularities, the harmonised benchmark table clamps each sub-region's pre-colonisation entries to its earliest positive anchor (for example, 8k for the Society Islands and 6k for the Marquesas prior to AD 500), yielding a harmonised nominal start of 35,7k at 1000BC and 65,2k at AD 1. Both series converge identically once all nine archipelagos are populated after AD 1000 and match exactly at the closing 1800 horizon (213,4k).

## Four-Wave Settlement Gazetteer Assembly

In parallel with regional archipelago totals, AUSTRAL assembles an evidence-based gazetteer of 67 catalogued pre-colonial settlements containing 184 dated population observations (mean 2,75 observations per settlement) across all ten modern national and territorial jurisdictions. Every settlement record derives strictly from documented archaeological, ethnohistorical or colonial census sources, with a crowd-sourced fallback share of exactly 0% across every sub-region.

Gazetteer construction proceeded across four sequential ingestion waves audited in the chapter source ledger. Wave 1 harvested 9 foundational entries anchored in official national and colonial statistical registries across Tonga, Samoa, French Polynesia, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tuvalu, Tokelau and Pitcairn. Wave 2 supplied 57 core pre-colonial chiefdom capitals, valley complexes, fortified refuges and founder excavations from peer-reviewed archaeological monographs and ethnohistorical surveys, covering sites from Lapita Nukuleka and Mulifanua to monumental Mu'a, Pulemelei, Taputapuātea, Opunohu, Taipivai, Anakena and Tongariki. Wave 3 conducted longitudinal reconciliation and duplicate elimination, verifying zero redundant aliases or split districts across the 67 locales. Wave 4 executed a targeted sub-regional coverage sweep that added 1 final verification entry (marginal gain 1,52%, well below the 2% saturation ceiling), confirming zero empty sub-regions and zero unaccounted candidate sites. Every included locale is assigned a uniform city-proper or single-valley chiefdom spatial scope so that local settlement headcounts never double-count whole-island rural totals.

# Testing and Validation

## Reconciliation Against Historical GIS Regimes and Radiocarbon Synthesis

Two independent cross-checks verify the internal consistency of our archipelago series: comparison against the 89-row Historical GIS (HGIS) territorial regime panel spanning AD 1 to 1800, and alignment with modern radiocarbon and genomic chronologies [@wilmshurst2011high; @ioannidis2021paths; @dinapoli2021approximate]. Across the six shared post-AD 1 snapshots, the HGIS territorial panel tracks 11 inhabited units totalling 51,1k at AD 1, rising across 13 units to 74,8k at AD 500, 114k at AD 1000, 189k at AD 1500, 223,9k at AD 1700 and a pre-contact crest of 233k (232.955) in 1780 before retreating under early introduced epidemics to 211,7k (211.748) in 1800. Our harmonised regional series stands within 3,1% of the HGIS panel at AD 500 (77,1k vs 74,8k), tracks smoothly through AD 1000 (126,5k vs 114k) and AD 1400 (193,2k vs 189k in 1500) and closes within 0,77% at 1800 (213,4k vs 211,7k).

A third diagnostic checks spatial raster coverage against polygon totals. On the coarse global raster grid, only the larger high-island blocks of Tonga (36k in 1800) and Independent Samoa (42k in 1800) resolve cleanly at sub-pixel scale, yielding a rasterised domain sum of 78k in 1800 (36,6% of the 213,4k archipelago total). Smaller eastern volcanic islands and narrow coral atoll rings in the Society, Marquesas, Cook, Austral, Tuamotu, Tuvalu, Tokelau and Rapa Nui zones fall below continental raster cell widths and are therefore retained strictly through vector polygon integration and settlement-point allocation rather than raw raster cell summation.

## Radiocarbon Chronology and Rapa Nui Demographic Calibration

Recent Bayesian recalibrations of Pacific radiocarbon databases impose stringent bounds on both the onset of East Polynesian growth and the contentious demographic trajectory of Rapa Nui [@wilmshurst2011high; @petchey2020vital; @dinapoli2021approximate]. For West Polynesia, uranium-thorium dates on Nukuleka coral abraders anchor Lapita founding firmly in the ninth century BC [@burley2012high], matching our 1000BC Tonga-Samoa baseline of 4,5k and rapid expansion to 34k by AD 1. For East Polynesia, strict removal of inbuilt-age charcoal and uncorrected marine shell samples compresses initial colonisation into the tenth to thirteenth centuries AD [@wilmshurst2011high; @petchey2010interpreting]. Our raw archipelago anchors reflect a conservative transitional spread—capturing the earliest contested Society and Marquesas horizons alongside the main AD 1000 to 1400 demographic take-off during which Society Islands population climbed nearly fivefold (8k to 38k by 1200) and Marquesan population surged from 6k to 28k [@allen2022lost; @molle2011perspectives].

On Rapa Nui, Approximate Bayesian Computation of radiocarbon and palaeoenvironmental records rejects older dramatic claims of a catastrophic pre-contact "ecocide" collapse from 20k or 30k people down to near-extinction before Jacob Roggeveen's arrival in 1722 [@dinapoli2021approximate]. Instead, lithic-mulch agricultural productivity and decentralised *moai* quarry workshop studies at Rano Raraku indicate that Rapa Nui supported a resilient low-to-moderate chiefdom population peaking in the high single thousands before declining under late pre-contact aridity and eighteenth-century contact shocks [@lipo2025megalithic; @dinapoli2021approximate]. Our sub-regional series—peaking at 9,5k in 1550 and easing to 3,2k by 1800 (combining Rapa Nui with Pitcairn's 27 residents)—sits squarely inside the upper sustainable envelope while reflecting eighteenth-century contraction prior to the devastating Peruvian slave raids of the 1860s.

# Results

## Oceanic Demographic Trajectory (1000BC to 1800)

Polynesian demographic expansion unfolded in three distinct phases across nearly three millennia: a West Polynesian formative build-up during the first millennium BC and first millennium AD, an explosive East Polynesian high-island surge between AD 1000 and AD 1770, and an uneven early-contact inflection during the closing three decades of the eighteenth century (Figure \ref{fig:poly-trajectory}). On the continuous regional benchmark curve, aggregate population rose from 35,7k at 1000BC (4,5k raw West Polynesian baseline) to 65,2k at AD 1 (34k raw West Polynesia), 77,1k at AD 500, 100,1k at AD 800 and 126,5k at AD 1000. Between AD 1000 and AD 1400—the core centuries of East Polynesian valley intensification—total population added 66,7k inhabitants (+52,8%), reaching 193,2k (compound growth 0,106% per annum). Growth continued into the late eighteenth century, cresting around 233k across the HGIS regime series in 1780 (with asynchronous high-island peaks summing above 245k across the Society Islands in 1770 and the Marquesas in 1790) before early epidemic losses in central French Polynesia brought the 1800 closing total to 213,4k.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:poly-trajectory">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_austral/1.0-precolonial-polynesia/precolonial_polynesia_population_trajectory.png" alt="fig:poly-trajectory" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Harmonised demographic trajectory for Pre-Colonial Polynesia and its four largest archipelago sub-regions from 1000BC to 1800 (Panel A) and sub-regional buffered-mask population density rankings in 1800 (Panel B).</figcaption>
</figure>

Internal regional shares shifted markedly as the eastern archipelagos filled. At AD 1, Tonga and Independent Samoa with Wallis-Futuna accounted for 100% of archaeologically confirmed Polynesian population (and 52,1% even of the back-filled harmonised total). By AD 1000, West Polynesia still held 49% of the harmonised aggregate (62k of 126,5k), while the Society Islands (24,3k, 19,3%) and Marquesas (18k, 14,3%) were rising swiftly. By AD 1400, East Polynesia had overtaken the western homeland: the Society Islands (46,6k, 24,1%) stood as Polynesia's single most populous archipelago ahead of Samoa and Wallis-Futuna (39,5k, 20,5%), the Marquesas (32,9k, 17%) and Tonga (31,7k, 16,4%). That balance peaked around 1770, when Tahiti and its leeward neighbours reached 68k—nearly 29% of the entire region—before introduced respiratory, venereal and dysenteric pathogens cut the Society Islands by 38% to 42k in 1800 and nudged Independent Samoa with Wallis-Futuna (46k, 21,6%) back into first place at the close of the pre-colonial epoch.

## West Polynesia: Tonga, Samoa and Wallis-Futuna

Independent Samoa and Wallis-Futuna (6.338 km² mask footprint) expanded steadily from 2k Lapita pioneers in 1000BC to 18k in AD 1, 34k in AD 1000, 39,5k in AD 1400 and 46k in 1800 (7,26 inhabitants per km² of mask area, second highest in Polynesia). Unlike the Society Islands, Samoa experienced only brief eighteenth-century European contact (Roggeveen in 1722, Bougainville in 1768 and La Pérouse's deadly clash at Tutuila in 1787), sparing Upolu and Savai'i from major epidemic collapse prior to the missionary era of the 1830s [@gallagher2022investigatin; @weisler2016colonisation]. Settlement across the nine catalogued locales in this sub-region concentrated along the fertile coastal plains and inland volcanic basins of Upolu—led by Leulumoega (2,68k in 1780), Falefa (2,38k in 1800), Vailele (1,89k in 1800), Mulifanua (1,48k in 1800) and Luatuanu'u (1,42k in 1750)—paired with Savai'i's inland ceremonial hub at Pulemelei (1,68k in 1500) and northern coastal seat at Safotu (1,64k in 1750). On Uvea and Futuna, irrigated taro terraces at Sigave (1,36k in 1780) and the Tongan-built basalt fort complex at Talietumu (1,89k in 1780) anchored roughly 3,5k to 4k residents by 1800 [@gallagher2022investigatin].

The Tonga Archipelago (5.173,1 km² mask area) traced an equally durable trajectory, rising from 2,5k in 1000BC (anchored at the Nukuleka founder settlement on Tongatapu [@burley2012high; @burley2010nukuleka]) to 16k in AD 1, 28k in AD 1000, 31,7k in AD 1400 and 36k in 1800 (6,96 inhabitants per km² of mask area, third overall). Fertile volcanic ash soils mantling uplifted limestone platforms on Tongatapu, Vava'u and 'Eua supported intensive yam, taro and plantain gardens without steep erosion risk. Across Tonga's eight catalogued locales, the Tu'i Tonga royal capital at Mu'a led all of Pre-Colonial Polynesia at 4,1k inhabitants in 1777, supported by major regional seats at Neiafu on Vava'u (2,48k in 1793), Kolovai (2,24k in 1777) and Pea (1,85k in 1777) on Tongatapu, Pangai on Lifuka in Ha'apai (1,97k in 1777), Hihifo on Niuatoputapu (1,18k in 1616, an obsidian and exchange gateway to Samoa [@reepmeyer2012obsidian]), Nukuleka (935 in 1500) and Ohonua on 'Eua (890 in 1773).

## Central East Polynesia: Society Islands and the Marquesas

The Society Islands (6.400,3 km² mask area) achieved the highest pre-contact demographic concentration in our entire domain. Settled permanently by East Polynesian voyagers around the tenth to eleventh centuries [@wilmshurst2011high; @hudjashov2018investigatin], early coastal stations such as Fa'ahia on Huahine (325 in 950, rising to 690 in 1400) and Maupiti (260 in 1000 to 945 in 1769) gave way to dense terraced valleys and coastal chiefdoms across Tahiti, Mo'orea, Ra'iātea, Huahine and Bora Bora [@kahn2013residential]. Population rose from 8k in the AD 500 anchor to 38k in 1200 and peaked at 68k in 1770, shortly after Samuel Wallis (1767), Louis-Antoine de Bougainville (1768) and James Cook (1769) anchored at Matavai Bay. Four of Polynesia's seven largest recorded pre-colonial centres clustered within Windward Tahiti and Mo'orea alone: Pare-Arue at Matavai Bay (3,95k in 1769, seat of the rising Pomare dynasty), Papara on the south coast (3,45k in 1769, stronghold of the Teva lineage and the monumental *marae* Mahaiatea), the deeply surveyed Opunohu Valley on Mo'orea (3,24k in 1769 [@kahn2013residential]) and Tautira on the Tahiti Iti peninsula (2,89k in 1769). Across the Leeward Islands, Vaitape on Bora Bora (2,18k), Maeva on Huahine (1,79k) and the pan-Polynesian ritual centre of Taputapuātea on Ra'iātea (1,62k) anchored flourishing *ari'i* polities [@allen2025reciprocity; @mcgloin2026microwear]. Repeated European anchorage after 1767 unleashed devastating waves of dysentery, pulmonary infections and venereal infertility, slashing Pare-Arue to 2,45k, Papara to 2,1k and Tautira to 1,62k by 1797 and pulling the archipelago down by 26k people to 42k in 1800 (6,56 inhabitants per km²).

North-east across the Tuamotu barrier, the Marquesas Islands (3.475,2 km² mask area) registered the highest archipelago-envelope density in Polynesia in 1800 at 10,94 inhabitants per km² (38k people, down from a 1790 crest of 45k). Twelfth-century landfalls documented at Ha'atuatua on Nuku Hiva, Hane and Hatuana on Ua Huka and Hanamiai on Tahuata triggered rapid woodland clearance and agricultural valley filling [@allen2022lost; @molle2011perspectives]. Because steep basalt ridges isolated each catchment and narrow marine shelves restricted reef lagoons, Marquesans combined breadfruit agro-forestry with offshore pelagic fisheries documented as far north as the Eiao basalt quarry island [@lambrides2018taxonomic; @allen2025reciprocity]. By 1798, the three largest valley confederations—Taipivai on Nuku Hiva (3,85k), Atuona on Hiva Oa (3,12k) and Hakahau on Ua Pou (2,64k)—ranked among the ten most populous settlements in Polynesia, supplemented by Ha'atuatua (1,36k), Hane (1,42k in 1700) and Hanamiai (1,19k in 1774). Later contact exposure than Tahiti delayed full demographic collapse until the nineteenth-century whaling and smallpox decades, leaving 38k inhabitants in 1800.

## Southern Volcanic Arcs and Coral Atoll Archipelagos

South and west of the Society core, the Cook Islands and Niue (5.100 km² mask area) grew steadily from 6,5k in AD 800 to 16k in AD 1400 and 21k in 1800 (4,12 inhabitants per km²), recorded across ten catalogued locales—the largest regional site count in our gazetteer. On volcanic Rarotonga, three traditional *vaka* districts—Ngati Tiare (2,28k in 1790), Ngatangiia (1,86k in 1700) and Arorangi (1,64k in 1750)—encircled the interior mountain core along an ancient paved ring road (*Ara Metua*). On raised-limestone Mangaia, irrigated taro swamps fed by interior volcanic streams sustained Oneroa (2,65k in 1777) despite fierce inter-tribal competition, while Aitutaki's lagoon-rimmed Ureia (1,96k in 1790), Ma'uke's Anai'o (840), Mitiaro (265) and northern atoll Rakahanga (365) illustrate the archipelago's ecological breadth [@allen2025reciprocity; @ioannidis2021paths]. Isolated raised-atoll Niue, positioned between Tonga and the Cooks, supported two principal settlement clusters at Alofi (2,18k in 1774) and Mutalau (1,42k in 1774).

Along Polynesia's southern subtropical margin, the Austral Islands (4.987,2 km² mask area) climbed from 4k in AD 1000 to 9,5k in AD 1500 and 11k in 1800 (2,21 inhabitants per km²). Excavations of domestic stone enclosures on Rurutu and monumental *marae* on Ra'ivavae and Tubuai confirm densely settled valley chiefdoms linked into Central East Polynesian basalt and pearl-shell exchange [@kahn2026morphologica; @allen2025reciprocity; @mcgloin2026microwear]. Four Austral volcanic centres exceeded 1,8k inhabitants on the eve of contact: Moerai on Rurutu (2,42k in 1790), Rairua on Ra'ivavae (2,35k in 1775), Mataura on Tubuai (2,15k in 1789) and fortified Ahurei on cool, wind-swept Rapa Iti (1,85k in 1791), where steep taro terraces and ridge-top *pare* forts protected communities near the southern thermal limit of tropical root crops [@barber2021archaeologic].

Across the vast low coral archipelagos, hydrological limits enforced starkly lower densities. The Tuamotu and Gambier Islands occupy 28.160,4 km² of buffered mask area—44,7% of our entire regional footprint—yet supported only 11k inhabitants in 1800 (0,39 inhabitants per km², 28 times lower than the Marquesas). Most Tuamotuan atolls housed small kin groups shifting between motu islets, with only fertile, coconut-rich Anaa (Tukuhora, 1,84k in 1769, a formidable warrior atoll projecting raids across the western Tuamotus) and large lagoon passes such as Tiputa on Rangiroa (1,18k), Rotoava on Fakarava (720) and Otepa on Hao (640) supporting substantial villages. In the volcanic Gambier group at the southeastern end of the chain, Mangareva and Kamaka (620 in 1797, grouped on the southern boundary of the Austral-Gambier mask) served as the vital launching hub for Pitcairn, Henderson and Rapa Nui before late-contact missionary restructuring reshaped the islands [@flexner2026islands; @allen2025reciprocity]. Similarly, the coral atolls of Tuvalu and Tokelau (2.550,2 km² mask area) rose gradually from 2k in AD 500 to 4,2k in AD 1200 and 5,2k in 1800 (2,04 inhabitants per km²), distributed across nine compact atoll villages led by Lolua on Nanumea (980), Asau on Vaitupu (940), Kulia on Niutao (680), Fakaofo in Tokelau (680), Fongafale on Funafuti (560) and Nanumaga (545), alongside Nukunonu (420), Atafu (340) and Nukulaelae (295) [@petchey2010interpreting].

## Rapa Nui and Pitcairn: The Southeastern Horizon

Occupying 845,9 km² of mask area at the extreme eastern rim of Polynesia, Rapa Nui and Pitcairn follow a distinct boom-and-adjustment curve: zero at 1000BC, 1,2k by AD 1000 (marking early colonisation onset), surging to 9,5k at the peak of coastal *ahu* and *moai* construction around 1550 before contracting to 3,2k in 1800 (3,78 inhabitants per km²) [@dinapoli2021approximate; @lipo2025megalithic]. Five catalogued Rapa Nui territorial complexes document this shift from monumental ancestral coastal platforms to late-period seasonal ritual centres: Tongariki on the southeast Hotu Iti coast (1,14k in 1550, easing to 860 in 1722), Vaihu (920 in 1600 to 710 in 1722), the royal Miru seat at Anakena (840 in 1550 to 680 in 1722), the finely dressed masonry sanctuary of Vinapu (610 in 1650 to 440 in 1722) and the ceremonial birdman (*tangata manu*) cliff village of Orongo overlooking Rano Kau, which actually expanded from 460 in 1600 to 580 in 1722 as ritual authority pivoted away from giant statue transport [@lipo2025megalithic; @mathiesen2020disputa]. Farther west along the same oceanic corridor, Pitcairn's prehistoric basalt-quarry settlement at Bounty Bay peaked at 145 inhabitants around 1300 before regional voyaging contraction forced total abandonment after 1450; permanent habitation resumed only in 1790 with 27 founders at Adamstown [@allen2025reciprocity; @buhring2020archaeology].

## Settlement Hierarchy and Chiefdom Rank-Size Structure

Pre-colonial Polynesian political geography never generated dense commercial cities or bureaucratic capitals of ten thousand people. Even the largest royal seats—Mu'a on Tongatapu (4,1k), Pare-Arue (3,95k) and Papara (3,45k) on Tahiti, and Taipivai (3,85k) on Nuku Hiva—remained dispersed agro-maritime chiefdom agglomerations strung along lagoons, valley floors and ceremonial precincts [@kahn2013residential; @burley2018early]. Figure \ref{fig:poly-hierarchy} presents the twelve largest recorded settlements alongside the log-log rank-size curve across all 67 catalogued locales.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:poly-hierarchy">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_austral/1.0-precolonial-polynesia/precolonial_polynesia_urban_hierarchy.png" alt="fig:poly-hierarchy" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Twelve largest catalogued pre-colonial settlements (Panel A) and rank-size distribution across 67 Polynesian habitation locales with upper-tail power-law fit ($\alpha = 0,31$, $R^2 = 0,95$ across the top 33 centres, Panel B), 1000BC to 1800.</figcaption>
</figure>

Because ocean gaps fragmented political authority across dozens of self-sufficient islands and valleys, the settlement-size distribution is markedly flatter than a classical continental Zipf slope ($\alpha = 1$). Across the leading 33 volcanic chiefdom centres (4.100 down to 1.480 inhabitants), peak populations follow a tight power law with exponent $\alpha = 0,31$ ($R^2 = 0,95$), reflecting parity among rival island paramountcies in Tonga, Samoa, Tahiti, the Marquesas, the Cooks and the Australs. Below rank 33, the curve bends steeply downward (full 67-site slope $-0,72$, $R^2 = 0,58$) as it enters small Rapa Nui coastal lineages, outer coral atolls of Tuvalu, Tokelau and the Tuamotus (265 to 980 inhabitants) and marginal Pitcairn (145 prehistorically; 27 in 1790). Table \ref{tab:regional-shares} pairs each sub-region's evolving share of Polynesian population with its catalogued settlement count and leading recorded centre.

# Limitations

Four structural uncertainties qualify pre-colonial demographic estimates across Polynesia.

First, contact-era population baselines for the Society Islands and the Marquesas remain vigorously debated among historical demographers. Eighteenth-century navigators rarely penetrated interior valleys and often extrapolated from ceremonial canoe fleets or coastal crowds; Cook's botanist Johann Reinhold Forster estimated Tahiti alone at 120k to 200k, whereas twentieth-century demographic revisions anchored in early missionary counts and age-structure back-projection reduced the Society Islands to 35k to 70k and the Marquesas to 35k to 50k [@kahn2013residential; @allen2022lost]. Our figures of 68k for the Society Islands in 1770 (falling to 42k in 1800) and 45k for the Marquesas in 1790 (38k in 1800) follow modern archaeological carrying-capacity and critical ethnohistorical consensus, yet plausible uncertainty bands of $\pm 20\%$ persist across late eighteenth-century totals.

Second, radiocarbon chronology across East Polynesia and central coral atolls remains sensitive to marine reservoir offsets and inbuilt wood age [@wilmshurst2011high; @petchey2010interpreting; @petchey2020vital]. Shifting initial East Polynesian arrival by two centuries—for instance from AD 900 to AD 1100 in the Societies or Marquesas—compresses early founding growth rates without altering late pre-colonial carrying capacities, though it leaves pre-AD 1000 regional totals inherently provisional. Furthermore, the harmonised continuous benchmark series back-fills East Polynesian initial positive anchors before AD 500 to preserve log-linear continuity across all nine sub-regions; readers examining the 1000BC and AD 1 columns must distinguish the harmonised nominal series (35,7k and 65,2k) from the archaeologically attested West Polynesian population (4,5k and 34k).

Third, coarse continental raster masks cannot resolve tiny volcanic islands or ribbon-like coral atolls without generous coastal buffering. While our 63.030,3 km² mask footprint enables consistent cartographic and cross-regional spatial integration across all nine archipelagos, mask-envelope densities (such as 0,39 inhabitants per km² in Tuamotu-Gambier or 3,39 overall) substantially understate true terrestrial pressure on scarce arable soils, particularly on crowded atolls and irrigated high-island valleys. Similarly, the polygon boundary separating the Gambier and Austral masks assigns Kamaka to the southern Austral-Gambier mask count (5 sites) rather than the Tuamotu-Gambier count (4 sites), a minor cartographic boundary effect with zero impact on total population.

Fourth, archaeological excavation intensity varies sharply between heavily studied hubs—Tongatapu, Upolu, Mo'orea, Nuku Hiva, Ua Huka, Rurutu and Rapa Nui—and lightly surveyed outer atolls in the Tuamotus, Northern Cooks, Tuvalu and Tokelau [@kahn2026morphologica; @molle2011perspectives; @petchey2010interpreting]. Late pre-colonial headcounts on remote atolls therefore lean more heavily on backward projection from early nineteenth-century missionary counts and twentieth-century colonial censuses, tempered by explicit adjustment for the 1862 to 1863 Peruvian slaving raids and nineteenth-century epidemics.

# Conclusion

Over nearly three millennia from the Lapita founding of Nukuleka around 888BC to the threshold of colonial annexation in 1800, Polynesian voyagers transformed the central and eastern Pacific into a network of self-sustaining island societies. From roughly 4,5k settlers in West Polynesia at 1000BC and 34k by AD 1, indigenous population across our nine archipelago sub-regions expanded past 126k by AD 1000, reached 193,2k by AD 1400 and crested near 233k on the eve of sustained European contact in 1770 to 1780, before early introduced epidemics in central French Polynesia brought the closing 1800 total to 213,4k [@burley2012high; @wilmshurst2011high; @ioannidis2021paths].

Geography and agro-ecology governed every tier of that human landscape. High volcanic archipelagos—Independent Samoa and Wallis-Futuna (46k in 1800), the Society Islands (42k, down from 68k in 1770), the Marquesas (38k, down from 45k in 1790), Tonga (36k) and the Cook Islands with Niue (21k)—held 85,8% of Polynesia's inhabitants in 1800 and nurtured every chiefdom agglomeration above two thousand people, from Tu'i Tonga's royal port at Mu'a (4,1k) to Pare-Arue (3,95k), Taipivai (3,85k) and Papara (3,45k). Across the vast coral atoll belts of the Tuamotus, Tuvalu and Tokelau and the windswept volcanic margins of Rapa Nui and Rapa Iti, scarce freshwater, cyclone surges and thermal limits capped village size yet fostered remarkable adaptive resilience, from lithic-mulch sweet-potato gardens on Rapa Nui to pan-archipelago exchange networks linking pearl shell, basalt adzes and sacred ritual lineages across thousands of kilometres of open sea [@allen2025reciprocity; @dinapoli2021approximate; @barber2021archaeologic]. By 1800, however, the long pre-colonial demographic equilibrium had already fractured in Tahiti and the Marquesas—foreshadowing the severe nineteenth-century epidemic depopulation that would sweep every Polynesian archipelago in the century ahead.

# Footnotes

All numerical values follow European decimal formatting (comma decimals and dot thousands separators) paired with semantic magnitude suffixes (k for thousands). Calendar dates prior to AD 1 are denoted with attached BC notation without thousands dots (1000BC), and post-AD dates follow AD prefixing where helpful for chronological clarity. Territory exclusions reflect macro-regional boundary assignments in AUSTRAL: Hawai'i and American Samoa are assigned to the United States Pacific territorial series, while Aotearoa New Zealand is treated in its own pre-European companion chapter.
